IB Computer Science

Explore the course by theme, topic, and subtopic.

IB Computer Science is a two-year course in which students study how computer systems work, how software is designed, and how computational thinking is used to solve real problems. The course combines theory with practical problem-solving and programming, and is organised into two main areas: Concepts of computer science and Computational thinking and problem-solving. It is available at both Standard Level (SL) and Higher Level (HL).

What You Study

The course is split into two themes.

Theme A

Concepts of Computer Science

This part of the course focuses on the theory behind computer systems, including how computers process data, how networks communicate, how databases are designed and queried, and how machine learning systems are developed and evaluated.

A1

Computer Fundamentals

Core principles that underpin the operation of a computer system.

  • A1.1 Computer hardware and operation
  • A1.2 Data representation and computer logic
  • A1.3 Operating systems and control systems
  • A1.4 Translation HL
SL: 11h | HL: 18h A2

Networks

How computers communicate and how modern networks are structured and secured.

  • A2.1 Network fundamentals
  • A2.2 Network architecture
  • A2.3 Data transmissions
  • A2.4 Network security
SL: 11h | HL: 18h A3

Databases

The storage, organisation and retrieval of data.

  • A3.1 Database fundamentals
  • A3.2 Database design
  • A3.3 Database programming
  • A3.4 Alternative databases and data warehouses HL
SL: 11h | HL: 18h A4

Machine Learning

Machine learning and some of the issues involved in building and using ML systems.

  • A4.1 Machine learning fundamentals
  • A4.2 Data preprocessing HL
  • A4.3 Machine learning approaches HL
  • A4.4 Ethical considerations
SL: 5h | HL: 18h

Theme B

Computational Thinking and Problem-Solving

This part of the course focuses more directly on designing solutions, writing programs, and using computational thinking to analyse and solve problems.

B1

Computational Thinking

The ways computer scientists think about problems and solutions.

  • B1.1 Approaches to computational thinking
SL: 5h | HL: 5h B2

Programming

The largest part of the course — practical programming knowledge needed to create working solutions.

  • B2.1 Programming fundamentals
  • B2.2 Data structures
  • B2.3 Programming constructs
  • B2.4 Programming algorithms
  • B2.5 File processing
SL: 40h | HL: 42h B3

Object-Oriented Programming

Object-oriented design and programming.

  • B3.1 Fundamentals of OOP for a single class
  • B3.2 Fundamentals of OOP for multiple classes HL
SL: 7h | HL: 23h B4

Abstract Data Types

An additional HL-only unit covering linked lists, binary search trees, sets and hashing.

  • B4.1 Fundamentals of ADTs HL
HL Only | 23h

Assessment

The course is assessed through external examinations and one internal assessment task. At SL, external assessment makes up 70% of the final grade and the internal assessment makes up 30%. At HL, external assessment makes up 80% and the internal assessment makes up 20%.

Paper 1

Based on Theme A: Concepts of computer science and the pre-seen case study. Split into two sections.

SL 1h 15m — 35% of final grade
HL 2h — 40% of final grade
  • Section A: Extended-response questions linked to Theme A
  • Section B: Questions linked to the pre-seen case study

Paper 2

Based on Theme B: Computational thinking and problem-solving.

SL 1h 15m — 35%
HL 2h — 40%

Extended-response questions linked to Theme B. One SL question focuses on algorithmic thinking without requiring code.

Case Study

A pre-seen scenario based on current developments, emerging technologies and/or ethical issues in computer science. Students research it in advance and answer questions in Paper 1 Section B.

SL 2 challenge questions
HL 4 challenge questions

Published 12 months before the May session or 18 months before the November session.

Internal Assessment

The computational solution — a practical project where students identify a problem, develop a working computational solution, and document and evaluate what they have produced.

SL 30% of final grade
HL 20% of final grade

Internally assessed by the teacher, externally moderated by the IB.

Extended Essay

Computer Science can be chosen as an Extended Essay subject. The EE is an opportunity to carry out independent research — its emphasis is on research, analysis and argumentation, distinct from the practical IA.

Externally assessed. Optional.

In Summary

IB Computer Science covers computer systems, networks, databases, machine learning, computational thinking, programming, object-oriented programming and, at HL, abstract data types and additional depth across several topics. Assessment is split between two exam papers and one practical internal assessment, with the case study forming a specific part of Paper 1 and the computational solution forming the IA.
